title: A tiny BIST, end to end
summary: Time to put everything together: a **controller** starts the test, an **LFSR** makes the patterns, a small circuit answers, a **MISR** compacts the answers, and the result is compared with the **golden signature**. You will follow every clock and see a fault being caught.
objectives: Describe the states of a BIST controller.
Explain where the golden signature comes from and what fault coverage means.
Follow a complete BIST run clock by clock and see how a fault changes the signature.
Know what the MBIST and LBIST courses build on this.

blocks.md: The pattern generator and the MISR need someone to tell them **when** to start and **when** to stop. That is the job of a small finite-state machine, the **BIST controller**:

steps.title: IDLE
steps.md: The chip works normally. The BIST logic waits; its output **done** is 0.

steps.title: INIT
steps.md: The tester (or the chip's own software at power-on) raises **start**. The controller loads the **seed** into the LFSR, clears the MISR and the pattern counter, and switches the circuit's inputs to the LFSR.

steps.title: RUN
steps.md: On every clock the LFSR produces a new pattern, the circuit answers and the MISR takes the answers in. A counter counts the patterns.

steps.title: CHECK
steps.md: After exactly **N** patterns the controller stops the LFSR and the MISR and compares the MISR with the **golden signature**.

steps.title: DONE
steps.md: The controller raises **done** and sets **pass** to 1 or 0. When the tester has read the result and drops *start*, it returns to IDLE and the chip goes back to normal work.

blocks.title: Why count exactly N patterns?
blocks.md: The golden signature is valid only for the **same seed** and the **same number of patterns**. One clock more or less and even a perfect chip gives a different signature.

rows: connects the circuit to the LFSR and MISR instead of its normal inputs
blocks.caption: The controller's interface — in a real chip these are reached through JTAG

subsections.title: The golden signature and fault coverage

blocks.md: Where does the expected value come from? Before the chip is built, engineers **simulate** the fault-free design with exactly the BIST settings: same seed, same number of patterns. The final MISR value in the simulation is the **golden signature**. It is stored as a constant in the controller, or the tester reads the signature and compares it.

items.title: Fault simulation
items.md: The same simulation is repeated with one modelled fault at a time (for example, every line stuck-at-0 and stuck-at-1). If the final signature differs from the golden one, the fault is **detected**.

items.title: Fault coverage
items.md:
> fault coverage = detected faults ÷ all modelled faults

For production chips the target is usually well above **95 %** for stuck-at faults. If LBIST alone does not reach it, more patterns, test points or extra tester patterns are added.

items.title: Keep it up to date
items.md: Every change in the design (or in the seed or pattern count) changes the golden signature. It is regenerated automatically in the design flow — never typed in by hand.

steps.title: 1. Pattern generator
steps.md: A 3-bit LFSR from Topic 4 (new Q1 = Q2 ⊕ Q3), seed 100. It drives the inputs **a, b, c** and goes through all 7 non-zero patterns.

steps.title: 2. Circuit under test
steps.md: A tiny circuit with three outputs: **y1 = a AND b**, **y2 = b OR c**, **y3 = a XOR c**.

steps.title: 3. MISR
steps.md: The 4-bit MISR from Topic 5 takes y1, y2, y3 as D1, D2, D3 (D4 = 0). It starts at 0000.

steps.title: 4. Compare
steps.md: After the 7th pattern the MISR holds the signature. The golden value, from simulation, is **0110**.

steps.title: 5. Controller
steps.md: The controller from 6.1 runs everything: seeds the LFSR, clears the MISR, counts 7 patterns and reports done and pass.

blocks.md: Now run it — once fault-free, and once with a defect that makes **y1 stuck-at-0**:

blocks.caption: MISR states Q1Q2Q3Q4 after each clock. The faulty chip ends with 0101 ≠ 0110 → FAIL

blocks.title: Look at clock 6
blocks.md: In clock 6 the faulty MISR happens to show **0110** — the golden value — but the test is not over yet. Only the value after the **last** pattern counts; that is why the controller must stop at exactly N.

tabs.label: Fault coverage of the tiny BIST
tabs.md: Simulating all 12 stuck-at faults on the lines a, b, c, y1, y2, y3 (each stuck-at-0 and stuck-at-1): **all 12** give a signature different from 0110. Fault coverage = 12 ÷ 12 = **100 %**.

tabs.label: With a 3-bit MISR
tabs.md: Replace the MISR by a 3-bit one (x³ + x² + 1) and simulate again: **4 of the 12** faults (b stuck-at-0/1, y3 stuck-at-0/1) change the responses but end with the golden signature — **aliasing**. Coverage drops to 8 ÷ 12 ≈ 67 %. A narrow MISR is risky; real ones are 16–64 bits.

blocks.md: Check yourself: say the meaning, then flip the card.

cards.back: Built-in self-test: generator, circuit under test, response checker and controller on the chip.
Shift register with XOR feedback; with a primitive polynomial it runs through 2ⁿ − 1 states.
Signature register that compacts many response bits per clock into one signature.
The signature of the fault-free design, from simulation with the same seed and pattern count.
A faulty circuit produces the golden signature; probability ≈ 2⁻ⁿ.

tabs.label: Memory BIST course
tabs.md: Memories and their fault models, **March tests**, the MBIST controller and collar, test access over JTAG, diagnosis and **repair**. Instead of an LFSR and a MISR, MBIST uses address/data generators and a comparator — but the controller idea is the same.

tabs.label: Logic BIST course
tabs.md: LFSR + phase shifter feeding **scan chains**, a MISR at the outputs, X-bounding, test points and at-speed clocking — the full-size version of this topic's tiny BIST.

tabs.label: Labs
tabs.md: **Lab 1:** build and simulate the LFSR in SystemVerilog. **Lab 2:** build a MISR, inject faults and measure aliasing — the experiment you saw in the last tab.

questions.text: Put the states of the BIST controller in order.
Where does the golden signature come from?
options: From simulating the fault-free design with the same seed and number of patterns.
From the first chip that comes out of the factory.
From a random number chosen by the tester.

questions.text: Why must the controller stop after exactly N patterns?
options: The golden signature is valid only for that exact seed and pattern count.
The LFSR breaks after N patterns.
To save power in the MISR.

questions.text: In the walk-through, the MISR holds **0101** and the circuit outputs y1y2y3 = **010** (D4 = 0). Using Q1 = Q4 ⊕ D1, Q2 = Q1 ⊕ D2, Q3 = Q2 ⊕ D3, Q4 = Q3 ⊕ Q4, what is the next MISR state?
Fault simulation of a block with 50 modelled faults finds that 45 change the signature. What is the fault coverage?
In the tiny BIST, replacing the 4-bit MISR by a 3-bit MISR made some faults escape because of aliasing.
